description: Turma 27 de Sistemas de Informação da UFU - Universidade Federal de UberlândIA. Disparando 27 threads em paralelo para processar a realidade, quebrar barreiras lógicas e codificar soluções de outro mundo na órbita da NASA. 🚀🌌
summary:
firesync is a web platform that turns NASA fire data into decisions for fire commanders and crews. It shows where hot spots are burning now, whether that is normal for the place and time of year, and which areas carry the highest fire risk in the next 14 days.

It addresses the challenge by joining two sensor records into one. VIIRS records about six times more detections than MODIS, so we convert MODIS Aqua to the VIIRS scale with factors calibrated in the 13 years both sensors flew. The result is a consistent 24-year series, with estimated months marked and their uncertainty range available. A model trained only on past data estimates the 14-day risk per area: tested on the Amazon (2021-2024), it warned of 51 in 100 significant fire outbreaks, usually 10 days ahead.

It matters because commanders decide with little time. Knowing early where fire is likely can help place crews before it spreads. If early warning helped Amazon crews cut burned area as Cerrado brigades did (12%), that could mean about 290,000 hectares (710,000 acres) and 3.8 million tonnes of CO2 less in a year like 2024 (June to August): a hypothesis to test in a pilot.
details:
What it does and how it works

firesync answers three questions for the people who decide where to send fire crews: Where is fire burning now? Is it unusual for this place and time of year? Where is the risk highest in the next 14 days?

  • Fire now. A map of the last 24, 72 or 168 hours of NASA hot spots, as H3 hexagons (about 1,770 km² each) or points, with the intensity class of each detection. An icon marks the areas that are above the usual for the season (Attention and Critical).
  • Is it normal? The last 7 days and the month to date are compared with the median of the same dates (within ±15 days) in earlier VIIRS years. The alert level (Normal, Attention, Critical) follows rule v1, versioned in config/alert_rules.json.
  • Where next. A 14-day risk for every area, in four tiers (very high, high, medium, lower). The “Where to look first” list ranks areas by risk, and high-risk areas enter the list even when there is no fire there now.
  • 24-year calendar. The user draws an area (polygon or rectangle), picks one of the six biome regions, or types a point and radius, and sees a months × years calendar of fire detections from January 2003 on one scale. Estimated months (MODIS era) are hatched and carry an uncertainty range. A month with a satellite outage is shown as missing data, which is different from zero.
  • Ask the data. A chat assistant answers questions such as “is the Pantanal above normal this week?” in the language of the question. It does not write numbers itself. It calls the same API functions as the screen (calendar, recent window, map, risk), and every figure in the answer is checked against what those functions returned, with the sources shown.
  • Downloads. CSV tables, a PNG of the calendar and an audit package (ZIP) with the raw counts by cell, the conversion factors of every scenario, the formula and the filters, so anyone can rebuild the calendar.

How it works

  1. Data. NASA FIRMS active fire detections for Brazil since November 2000: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), from the yearly country files and the near-real-time API.
    • Standardized before counting. The FIRMS columns of both sensors are brought to one format: satellite name, acquisition date and UTC time, day or night pass (daynight), and the brightness columns, whose names change with the source. Confidence comes on different scales (MODIS 0 to 100, VIIRS low, nominal or high). MODIS is mapped to the same three classes (below 30 low, 30 to 79 nominal, 80 or more high), and the two scales are never compared directly.
      • Only vegetation fires (type 0) with fire power (FRP) above zero are kept.
      • Exact duplicates are removed.
      • Low-confidence detections are kept apart. VIIRS low-confidence night detections are dropped because of the South Atlantic Anomaly.
      • Pixel size (scan, track) is not filtered.
      • Only Aqua is used on the MODIS side, because it crosses at about the same time of day as S-NPP.
      • NOAA-20 is treated as equal to S-NPP.
      • Fire power is left out of the factor on purpose. In the MODIS-only years, the fires MODIS missed have no FRP recorded, and FRP is not comparable between the two sensors.
      • In the 13 overlap years (2012 to 2024), we count Aqua and S-NPP detections per H3 cell and divide the sums. This gives one factor per biome, month and pass for each year: 1,860 factors.
      • Days with a data gap in either satellite are left out.
      • A condition with too few detections borrows from the neighbouring months, then from the whole year.
      • A MODIS-era month is the median of the 13 scenarios, with a 5th to 95th percentile range.
    • It uses 10 variables, all from daily VIIRS detection counts per cell: fire in the last 7, 14 and 30 days, trend, neighbouring cells, the same season in earlier years, week of the year, and position.
    • It was trained only on earlier years and tested year by year.
    • A separate job writes the scores to the database, and the API only reads them.

Benefits

  • A decision aid for fire commanders and crews: which areas to look at first today, and where to prepare resources in the next 14 days.
  • Context, not just a map. Today’s fire is shown against what is normal for the place and the season, with 24 years of NASA data read as one series.
  • Honest numbers. Estimated months are marked and carry an uncertainty range. The alert rule is versioned, and every number can be rebuilt from the audit package.
  • Open and easy to reach: open source, no login, works on desktop and mobile, in English, with colour scales that are readable with colour-vision deficiency.

Intended impact

What we measured (Amazon, 2021 to 2024, with the model trained each year only on earlier years):

  • It warned of 51 in every 100 starts of significant fire (10 or more VIIRS detections in 14 days).
    • Of those, 42 were warned 3 days or more ahead and 33 7 days or more ahead.
    • Among the warned, the median lead time was 10 days.
    • 49 in every 100 still arrive without a warning.
  • When it flags an area (probability of 50% or more), significant fire followed in 78% of cases. It flagged 74% of the areas that had significant fire. In Brazil as a whole, the figures are 76% and 66%.
  • Looking only at the 20% of areas with the highest score each week, a brigade covers 66% of the significant fire. The top 10% of areas cover 42%. A random choice captures only as much as the share of areas chosen.
  • NASA’s burned-area product agrees: the “very high” tier holds 75.5% of the area burned in the next 14 days (see “How we checked it”).

What we estimate as a scenario, not as a result.

  • The inputs:
    • Brigades in conservation units of the Cerrado reduced burned area by about 12% (Oliveira et al., via Aliança da Terra and Embrapa).
    • The Amazon burned about 2.4 million hectares from June to August 2024, an extreme drought year (IPAM).
    • that the Cerrado effect also holds in the Amazon;
    • that warning ahead makes brigades more effective (the study measures having brigades, not having a warning);
    • that an average year would give less.
  • It is a hypothesis to test in a pilot with a fire brigade.

How we checked it

Every check had its pass or fail criterion fixed before the run, and we tried to refute each result before reporting it.

  • The harmonized series, year by year. We left one overlap year out, rebuilt the factors with the other years and compared the estimate with the real VIIRS count of the year left out. In the Amazon the error is about 6% a year, and the uncertainty range holds the real value about 8 times in 10.
    • Result: the two series have the same shape in all six biomes:
      • monthly correlation of 0.94 to 0.99;
      • the same peak month (within one month) in 83% to 100% of the years;
      • 4 or 5 of the 5 worst years in common.
    • The bias we declare: INPE’s series is almost Aqua itself (monthly correlation of 0.998). This comparison checks the shape of the curve and the 2012 sensor switch, not the size of the factor. The year-by-year test above is what checks the factor.
    • INPE is compared only by the shape of the curve, never by absolute value, because it counts on the scale of one satellite.
    • The 2012 switch leaves no artificial jump in the Amazon (−0.6%), and a jump of up to about 7% in the Cerrado, Caatinga and Pantanal. In the Atlantic Forest (−12.7%) and the Pampa (+12.3%) the step is larger, and we say so in the method.
    • Result: our model ranked areas better in every year.
      • 59% to 64% of its top 10% areas had significant fire, against 25% to 31% for INPE’s index.
      • AUC of 0.94 to 0.95, against 0.74 to 0.81.
      • in areas with no fire in the previous 30 days;
      • in each biome;
      • with 3-day and 7-day horizons;
      • with the cell maximum instead of the mean;
      • in each year apart.
    • This does not make INPE’s index a poor danger indicator: it answers a different question. Adding it to our model gave no gain, so it is an external benchmark and not an input.
    • The “very high” tier is 11% of the predictions and holds 75.5% of all the area burned in the following 14 days.
    • 69% of the places that burned had been flagged high or very high.
    • The score separates burned from unburned places with an AUC of 0.898, between 0.880 and 0.904 in each year.
    • This hit rate is a floor: MCD64A1 misses small burns and pixels under cloud or smoke.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data pipeline and models: Python (pandas, PyArrow, GeoPandas, pyogrio, Shapely, h3, psycopg, scikit-learn).
  • Database: PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4 and the Uber H3 grid.
  • API: Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn, in a hexagonal architecture.
  • Front end: TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet with Leaflet-Geoman, D3 (d3-scale, d3-scale-chromatic), GSAP, three.js for the opening globe, Archivo typeface.
  • Assistant: tool calling over the API’s use cases, through OpenAI-compatible chat completion APIs with a fallback chain of providers.
  • Tests and delivery: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright user journeys, GitHub Actions, Docker Compose, Cloudflare Workers and Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. The site is static, and the API and jobs run on one small virtual server.

The creative aspect

  • Joining two sensors without hiding the doubt. Instead of hiding the 2012 sensor switch, firesync converts MODIS to the VIIRS scale with 13 calibration scenarios. It hatches the estimated months on the calendar and gives each one an uncertainty range. The opening of the site shows the MODIS-to-VIIRS band folding into the calendar.
  • “Is this fire normal?” Today’s fire is compared with the same dates in earlier years, in plain language, with a verdict in one sentence.
  • Early warning for places with no fire yet. The risk list brings areas to the top before the first detection.
  • Everything can be rebuilt. A versioned alert rule and an audit package for every query let a judge or a scientist recompute the numbers.
  • A descent from the planet to the decision. The opening takes the user from the globe, with the Aqua and Suomi NPP satellites in orbit, down to a full-screen map with the tools of a commander.

Factors the team considered

  • Detections are not fires and not burned area. One large fire produces many detections. We count detections, and say so on screen.
    • 52% of the high-detection periods followed a week rated Normal.
    • 49 in every 100 starts of significant fire still arrive without a warning.
    • The risk model uses only VIIRS detection counts, with no weather forecast.
    • NASA POWER weather data and more MODIS history were tested. They did not improve the model under criteria fixed before the runs, so they are not in the product.
    • The Pantanal has few areas and an anomalous 2020, so its results carry a warning.
    • The model covers less outside the fire season (62% in the Amazon).
  • The conversion assumes the sensor ratio of 2003 to 2011 was similar to 2012 to 2024, which cannot be tested. In exceptional years (2020 and 2024 in the Amazon) the estimate errs more.
  • Sensor change. S-NPP is the VIIRS source until October 2026, and NOAA-20 from November 2026. The risk model was tested for the switch with no harm.
  • Independent references. The series and the risk model were compared with INPE and with NASA burned area, with the biases of each comparison declared (see “How we checked it”).
  • People under pressure. Large touch targets, shape and text besides colour, a colour scale readable with colour-vision deficiency, and no login.
  • The virtual assistant stays inside the data. It answers only with figures returned by our own API, and shows its sources.
  • A decision aid, not a decision. The tool ranks where to look. It does not replace field information, wind, or the judgment of the commander.

Next steps

  • Field updates from the fire line. A login area for fire commanders and crews to report the conditions of each fire in real time (active, controlled, out, front advancing). The map would then join what the satellite sees with what the crews see on the ground.
    • We tested the index as an input to the risk model, and it did not help: 13 years hold few El Niño episodes, and the effect differs by region.
    • It would enter as a clearly labelled “what if” scenario, not as part of the measured model.

Machine learning and AI tools

Machine learning inside the product. firesync uses two machine-learning models, both trained only on NASA data.

  • The 14-day risk model (gradient boosting, scikit-learn). It exists because a fixed rule cannot weigh ten fire signals at once across six biomes and every season.
    • Against the best simple rule we found (fire in the last 30 days plus the average of the same season), it gains about 2 points in the top 10% of areas, in 8 of 8 years.
    • Against INPE’s fire-risk index, it gains about 30 points.
    • The gain over the simple rule is small, and we say so. Most of the skill comes from recent fire, and new information (weather forecast, vegetation dryness) is what could raise it.
  • A detection classifier that learns the chance that MODIS saw each VIIRS fire, from fire power, temperature, confidence, month, day or night, biome and pixel size. It does not produce the conversion factor. It shows which fires MODIS misses (mostly the weak ones) and serves as a cross-check of the factor.

AI tools to build it.

  • The idea, the method and every pass or fail criterion are the team’s, and were fixed before the runs.
  • We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Antigravity and Lovable) to write and review code and documents from those decisions, test-first where possible.
  • Every change entered through a pull request with automated tests.
  • The AI-assisted parts are listed file by file in the “Uso de IA” table of the repository README.
  • No image, video or audio in the project or in the demo was generated by AI.
  • The optional virtual assistant in the site calls a language model at run time and gets every figure in its answers from our own API.

datasets/geo-countries (country boundaries in the opening globe)
